notes.front: What is cloud computing?
notes.back: Delivering computing services, such as virtual machines, storage, databases and networking, over the internet.
notes.explanation: Because the services arrive over the internet, growth is not tied to building physical datacentres of your own.
notes.example: Like renting a car by the day instead of buying one, but for servers and storage that you reach through the internet.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: What is cloud computing, “What is cloud computing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the shared responsibility model?
notes.back: The split of tasks, security tasks included, between the cloud provider and you, which changes with the type of deployment.
notes.explanation: On premises you own everything; moving to the cloud hands some of those responsibilities to Microsoft.
notes.example: Like renting a flat: the landlord keeps the building sound, but locking your own door and guarding your belongings stays with you.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Division of responsibility”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: In an on-premises datacenter, you own the whole stack. As you move to the cloud, some responsibilities transfer to Microsoft.

notes.front: What is a public cloud?
notes.back: Cloud services built, run and maintained by a third-party provider, which anyone who wants to buy them can use.
notes.explanation: Being open to the general public is the main thing that sets it apart from a private cloud.
notes.example: Like a public gym: one operator owns the equipment, and anyone who pays can use it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Public cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a private cloud?
notes.back: A cloud environment used by one organisation only, with its resources dedicated to that organisation.
notes.explanation: It grew out of the traditional datacentre: services still arrive over the internet, but nobody else shares the resources.
notes.example: Like a gym built inside one company’s office block, open only to that company’s staff.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Private cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a hybrid cloud?
notes.back: An environment that uses a public cloud and a private cloud together, connected to each other.
notes.explanation: Connecting the two lets you choose, service by service, which runs publicly and which stays private.
notes.example: Like a firm with its own delivery vans that hires extra vans from a rental company, and runs both from one dispatch desk.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Hybrid cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is multicloud?
notes.back: Using two or more public cloud providers, and managing resources and security in each of them.
notes.explanation: The training presents it as a fourth scenario beside the public, private and hybrid models.
notes.example: Like keeping accounts at two banks and handling each one’s cards and settings yourself.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure VMware Solution?
notes.back: An Azure service for running VMware workloads in Azure.
notes.explanation: It is aimed at organisations already running VMware in a private cloud that want to move to a public or hybrid cloud.
notes.example: Like moving house with all your furniture unchanged, instead of buying new furniture that fits the new rooms.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Azure VMware Solution”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the consumption-based model?
notes.back: Paying for the computing resources you actually use and nothing more, renting capacity and releasing it when done.
notes.explanation: You rent compute and storage instead of buying and running your own datacentre equipment.
notes.example: Like a metered electricity supply: the bill follows how much you used this month.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is capital expenditure (CapEx)?
notes.back: Up-front spending on physical infrastructure, such as servers, network hardware and datacentre space.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two traditional budgeting terms the training uses to classify cloud spending.
notes.example: Like buying a delivery van outright before you have made a single delivery.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is operational expenditure (OpEx)?
notes.back: Ongoing spending on services over time.
notes.explanation: It is the counterpart of capital expenditure in traditional budgeting.
notes.example: Like paying a courier firm each month for the deliveries it made, instead of owning the van.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is pay-as-you-go pricing?
notes.back: A pricing model in which you pay for the resources you used during a billing cycle.
notes.explanation: Use more in a cycle and the bill rises; use less and it falls, which gives the most flexibility.
notes.example: Like a mobile phone plan billed on the minutes you used, not a fixed bundle.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure, “Consumption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are Azure Reservations?
notes.back: A discount you get by committing to a one-year or three-year plan for particular products.
notes.explanation: The commitment is what earns the discount on the resources you use.
notes.example: Like a season ticket for one stand at one ground: cheaper than buying match by match, but tied to that seat.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “What are Azure Reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Reservations help you save money by committing to one-year or three-year plans for multiple products. Committing allows you to get a discount on the resources you use.

notes.front: What is Azure savings plan for compute?
notes.back: A commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour on eligible compute for one or three years, in return for lower prices.
notes.explanation: A savings plan is a commitment-based discount, and the compute plan covers a broad set of Azure compute services.
notes.example: Like a gift card you promise to top up by the same sum every hour, usable at any shop in one shopping centre.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “What are savings plans?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A savings plan is a commitment-based discount. You agree to spend a fixed dollar amount per hour for a set period (1 or 3 years), and in return you get lower prices on eligible usage.

notes.front: What are Azure Spot Virtual Machines?
notes.back: Virtual machines that run on Azure’s unused capacity at a large discount, and that Azure can evict when it needs the capacity back.
notes.explanation: The saving comes from using spare capacity, and the price of that is possible eviction at any time.
notes.example: Like a standby airline seat: cheap, but you lose it if a full-fare passenger turns up.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Spot Virtual Machines, “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Using Azure Spot Virtual Machines allows you to take advantage of our unused capacity at a significant cost savings. At any point in time when Azure needs the capacity back, the Azure infrastructure will evict Azure Spot Virtual Machines.

notes.front: What is serverless computing?
notes.back: Running code without maintaining virtual machines or containers; an event starts the code, and nothing stays provisioned between events.
notes.explanation: Resources behind a virtual machine or container must keep running for an app to work; serverless code is woken by events instead.
notes.example: Like a taxi you call only when you need a ride, instead of a car parked outside your door all day.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Describe Azure functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does growing quickly in the cloud not require building a new datacentre?
notes.back: Cloud services are delivered over the internet, so they are not bound by physical infrastructure the way a traditional datacentre is.
notes.explanation: That is why the cloud can expand an organisation’s capacity rapidly.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: What is cloud computing, “What is cloud computing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which responsibility you always retain covers data classification, data protection, encryption decisions and data-governance compliance?
notes.back: Data.
notes.explanation: Whatever the deployment type, your data remains yours to look after.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Data - You're responsible for your data, including data classification, data protection, encryption decisions, and compliance with data governance requirements.

notes.front: Which responsibility you always retain covers protecting the laptops, desktops and mobile devices that reach your cloud services?
notes.back: Endpoints.
notes.explanation: The devices that access your cloud services are yours to protect in every deployment type.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Endpoints - You're responsible for protecting client devices and endpoints that access your cloud services, including mobile devices, laptops, and desktops.

notes.front: Which responsibility you always retain covers creating, managing and removing user access?
notes.back: Accounts.
notes.explanation: Managing who has a user account stays with you whatever you deploy.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Accounts - You're responsible for managing user accounts, including creating, managing, and removing user access.

notes.front: Which responsibility you always retain covers implementing access controls such as role-based access control and conditional access policies?
notes.back: Access management.
notes.explanation: Setting and running the controls on who may do what stays with you in every deployment type.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Access management - You're responsible for implementing and managing access controls, including role-based access control (RBAC), multifactor authentication, and conditional access policies.

notes.front: Azure’s shared responsibility article lists {{c1::four}} responsibilities you always retain, whatever the type of deployment.
notes.explanation: They are data, endpoints, accounts and access management; the older training unit groups them into three.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Regardless of the type of deployment, you always retain the following responsibilities: - Data

notes.front: For all cloud deployment types, you own your {{c1::data and identities}}.
notes.explanation: You must protect them, together with any on-premises resources and the cloud components you control.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Division of responsibility”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: For all cloud deployment types, you own your data and identities. You're responsible for protecting the security of your data and identities, on-premises resources, and the cloud components you control.

notes.front: Which of Microsoft’s responsibilities covers datacentre facilities, physical access controls and environmental controls?
notes.back: Physical security.
notes.explanation: It is part of the underlying cloud infrastructure, which the article places with Microsoft.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Microsoft responsibilities”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Microsoft is responsible for the underlying cloud infrastructure, which includes: - Physical security - Securing datacenters, including facilities, physical access controls, and environmental controls.

notes.front: Which of Microsoft’s responsibilities covers the routers, switches and cables inside its datacentres?
notes.back: The physical network.
notes.explanation: Managing that network infrastructure is part of the cloud infrastructure Microsoft looks after.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Microsoft responsibilities”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Physical network - Managing network infrastructure, including routers, switches, and cables within datacenters.

notes.front: Which of Microsoft’s responsibilities covers managing and maintaining the physical servers that host cloud services?
notes.back: Physical hosts.
notes.explanation: The servers themselves belong to the underlying infrastructure that Microsoft runs.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Microsoft responsibilities”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Physical hosts - Managing and maintaining the physical servers that host cloud services.

notes.front: According to the training, why do physical security, power, cooling and connectivity sit with the cloud provider?
notes.back: The customer is not located with the datacentre, so holding those responsibilities would make no sense.
notes.explanation: The provider runs the building and the kit in it; the customer only reaches it remotely.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “How responsibilities shift in cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two things whose owner, under the shared responsibility model, depends on the type of cloud service you use?
notes.back: Two of: operating systems, network controls or applications.
notes.explanation: These sit between the parts you always keep and the parts the provider always runs.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “What depends on the service type”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In PaaS and SaaS, which part of identity and access do you manage, and which part does the provider run?
notes.back: The customer manages its own users, roles and policies; the provider runs the authentication platform.
notes.explanation: Managing users, roles and access policies stays with you in every model; what passes to the provider is the sign-in platform underneath.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “What depends on the service type”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do cloud models define, and what are the three main ones?
notes.back: The deployment type of cloud resources; the three main models are private, public and hybrid.
notes.explanation: Multicloud is described separately, as a further scenario.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where can a private cloud be hosted?
notes.back: In your own on-site datacentre, or in a dedicated off-site datacentre, possibly run by a third party.
notes.explanation: What makes it private is that its resources serve one organisation, not where the building stands.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Private cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Compared with a public cloud, what does a private cloud give up in exchange for greater control?
notes.back: It costs more and brings fewer of the public cloud’s benefits.
notes.explanation: The training presents greater control and greater cost as the two sides of the same choice.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Private cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can a hybrid cloud help a private cloud that faces a temporary rise in demand?
notes.back: It lets the private cloud surge by deploying public cloud resources for the extra load.
notes.explanation: The public side supplies the temporary capacity while the private side keeps running.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Hybrid cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two reasons an organisation may end up with multicloud?
notes.back: It uses different features from different providers; or it is migrating from one provider to another.
notes.explanation: Either way it has two or more public providers to manage, security included.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the training’s comparison table, the public cloud needs no {{c1::capital expenditures}} to scale up.
notes.explanation: You pay only for what you use, and applications can be provisioned and removed quickly.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models (comparison table)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the training’s comparison table, what must you buy and maintain with a private cloud?
notes.back: The hardware: it must be bought for start-up and maintenance, and you are responsible for its maintenance and updates.
notes.explanation: That hardware burden is the price of complete control over resources and security.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models (comparison table)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a private cloud, your data is not {{c1::collocated with other tenants’ data}}.
notes.explanation: The comparison table lists this beside complete control over resources and security.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models (comparison table)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which cloud model does the training’s comparison table say provides the most flexibility?
notes.back: The hybrid cloud.
notes.explanation: You decide where each application runs and control security, compliance or legal requirements yourself.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models (comparison table)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Because you pay for cloud services as you consume them, cloud computing is classified as {{c1::operational expenditure (OpEx)}}.
notes.explanation: Ongoing spending on services over time is the definition of operational expenditure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two benefits of the consumption-based model?
notes.back: Two of: no up-front hardware costs; no underused capacity to buy; adding resources as demand rises; releasing them as it falls.
notes.explanation: All follow from renting what you use instead of owning capacity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a traditional datacentre, what happens if you overestimate or underestimate future resource needs?
notes.back: Overestimate: you overspend on idle infrastructure. Underestimate: applications suffer degraded performance.
notes.explanation: Fixing a shortfall means ordering and installing more hardware, power and cooling.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Capacity planning: traditional vs. cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the training, what are two things that paying only for the services you consume helps you do?
notes.back: Two of: plan and manage operating costs; run infrastructure more efficiently; scale as workload needs change.
notes.explanation: The provider looks after power, cooling, hardware and networking, so you can focus on business problems.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Cloud pricing”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure Reservations commit you to a {{c1::one-year or three-year}} plan.
notes.explanation: The commitment is what earns the discount.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “What are Azure Reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Azure Reservations help you save money by committing to one-year or three-year plans for multiple products.

notes.front: By up to what percentage can reservations reduce resource costs compared with pay-as-you-go prices?
notes.back: Up to 72%.
notes.explanation: The documentation says “up to”, so 72% is a maximum.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “What are Azure Reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Reservations can significantly reduce your resource costs by up to 72% from pay-as-you-go prices.

notes.front: Does buying a reservation change how your resources run?
notes.back: No: it is a billing discount and does not affect the runtime state of your resources.
notes.explanation: After purchase, the discount simply applies automatically to matching resources.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “What are Azure Reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Reservations provide a billing discount and don't affect the runtime state of your resources. After you purchase a reservation, the discount automatically applies to matching resources.

notes.front: Does paying for a reservation monthly cost more in total than paying up front?
notes.back: No: the total cost is the same, with no extra fees for paying monthly.
notes.explanation: Up-front and monthly reservations have the same total cost.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “What are Azure Reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: You can pay for a reservation up front or monthly. The total cost of up-front and monthly reservations is the same and you don't pay any extra fees when you choose to pay monthly.

notes.front: With a savings plan, what exactly do you commit to?
notes.back: A fixed amount of spend per hour, for one or three years.
notes.explanation: Discounts vary by product and by term, not by the size of the commitment.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “What are savings plans?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: You agree to spend a fixed dollar amount per hour for a set period (1 or 3 years), and in return you get lower prices on eligible usage. Savings plan discounts vary by product and by commitment term (1- or 3-year), not the commitment amount.

notes.front: What happens to savings plan commitment that goes unused in a given hour?
notes.back: It expires and does not roll over.
notes.explanation: Benefits are applied hour by hour, so each hour’s commitment stands alone.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “How do savings plan discounts work?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Unused commitment for an hour expires and does not roll over.

notes.front: Eligible usage beyond a savings plan’s hourly commitment is billed at {{c1::regular pay-as-you-go rates}}.
notes.explanation: The discounted cost is deducted from the commitment first; only then does normal pricing apply.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “How do savings plan discounts work?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: any remaining eligible usage is billed at regular pay‑as‑you‑go rates once the commitment is fully used.

notes.front: Which three kinds of charge does savings plan for compute not cover?
notes.back: Software, networking and storage.
notes.explanation: It applies to infrastructure costs from eligible compute services.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “What savings plans are available”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Savings plan for compute doesn't cover software, networking, or storage charges.

notes.front: Can a savings plan purchase be cancelled or refunded?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The documentation states this as its cancellation and refund policy for savings plans.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “Cancellation and refund policy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Savings plan purchases can't be canceled or refunded.

notes.front: How much notice does Azure give before evicting a Spot virtual machine?
notes.back: 30 seconds.
notes.explanation: Azure evicts Spot machines whenever it needs the capacity back.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Spot Virtual Machines, “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: At any point in time when Azure needs the capacity back, the Azure infrastructure will evict Azure Spot Virtual Machines with 30-seconds notice.

notes.front: What are the two reasons a Spot virtual machine can be stopped?
notes.back: Azure needs the capacity for other pay-as-you-go workloads, or the spot price rises above the maximum price you set.
notes.explanation: Either condition triggers eviction under the policy you chose.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Spot Virtual Machines, “Eviction policy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Spot VMs can be stopped if Azure needs capacity for other pay-as-you-go workloads or when the price of the spot instance exceeds the maximum price that you have set.

notes.front: Which two eviction policies can you set on a Spot virtual machine, and which is the default?
notes.back: Deallocate (the default) or Delete.
notes.explanation: You choose the eviction policy when you create the Spot machine.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Azure Spot Virtual Machines, “Eviction policy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: When creating an Azure Spot Virtual Machine, you can set the eviction policy to *Deallocate* (default) or *Delete*.

notes.front: In the serverless model, what does Azure charge you for?
notes.back: Only the processor time used while your function runs.
notes.explanation: Resources are allocated when the code is triggered and released automatically when it finishes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do serverless functions respond to changing demand?
notes.back: They scale automatically based on demand.
notes.explanation: That may make them a good choice when demand is variable.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of work are serverless functions commonly used for?
notes.back: Work done in response to an event, timer or message that can be completed quickly, within seconds or less.
notes.explanation: The event wakes the function, so nothing needs to stay provisioned between events.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Benefits of Azure Functions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council’s bin-collection website gets ten times its usual traffic for one week after a timetable change. Using cloud computing, what should it do?
notes.back: Add cloud capacity for that week, then scale it back down afterwards.
notes.explanation: On-demand capacity avoids buying servers months ahead that sit idle for the rest of the year, keeping spending in line with demand.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: What is cloud computing, “Practical example”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A consultancy’s staff laptop, used to sign in to its cloud apps, is found to have no disk encryption or malware protection. Under the shared responsibility model, whose job was protecting it?
notes.back: B: the customer. Protecting endpoints that access cloud services is always the customer’s responsibility.
notes.choices:
A) Microsoft, because the laptop reaches Microsoft cloud services
B) The customer
C) Shared equally, whatever the deployment type
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: devices that reach cloud services stay the customer’s to protect. C is wrong: endpoint protection stays with the customer in every model; even in SaaS, where Microsoft may offer some device management, protecting the laptop is still the customer’s job.
notes.explanation: Endpoints, including laptops, are one of the responsibilities you retain in every deployment type.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Endpoints - You're responsible for protecting client devices and endpoints that access your cloud services, including mobile devices, laptops, and desktops.

notes.front: An employee left three months ago but can still sign in to the company’s cloud resources. Under the shared responsibility model, who failed?
notes.back: The customer: managing user accounts, including removing access, is always the customer’s job.
notes.explanation: Removing user access falls under accounts, one of the responsibilities you always retain.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Responsibilities you always retain”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Accounts - You're responsible for managing user accounts, including creating, managing, and removing user access.

notes.front: Customer or Microsoft? Replacing a faulty switch inside an Azure datacentre.
notes.back: Microsoft: the physical network within datacentres is Microsoft’s responsibility.
notes.explanation: Routers, switches and cables inside Azure datacentres are part of the physical network Microsoft manages.
notes.source: Azure documentation: Shared responsibility in the cloud, “Microsoft responsibilities”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Physical network - Managing network infrastructure, including routers, switches, and cables within datacenters.

notes.front: A team rents a cloud virtual machine and installs its own database engine on it. Who applies the database’s patches and updates?
notes.back: The team (the customer), who also keeps looking after the data stored in the database.
notes.explanation: Because the team installed the database itself, its upkeep falls to them; the training uses this to show that responsibility depends on the service.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “How responsibilities shift in cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team switches to a cloud database service that the provider runs. What does the provider now maintain, and what stays with the team?
notes.back: The provider maintains the database itself; the team stays responsible for the data that goes into it.
notes.explanation: Handing over the database does not hand over the data, which stays with the customer.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the shared responsibility model, “How responsibilities shift in cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A two-person start-up has no money for servers and wants to start and stop test environments within minutes, paying only for what it uses. Which cloud model fits best?
notes.back: B: public cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Private cloud
B) Public cloud
C) Hybrid cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a private cloud needs hardware bought up front. C is wrong: a hybrid cloud includes a private side the start-up has no reason to build.
notes.explanation: The public cloud needs no capital spending to scale, can provision and remove quickly, and charges only for use.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Define cloud models (comparison table)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A defence contractor needs complete control over its resources and security, and its data must never share hardware with other tenants. Which cloud model fits best?
notes.back: C: private cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Public cloud
B) Multicloud
C) Private cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a public cloud gives up complete control over resources and security. B is wrong: multicloud means several public providers, which does not meet either need.
notes.explanation: A private cloud gives complete control, and its data is not collocated with other tenants’ data.

notes.front: A tax office runs its own private cloud but needs extra capacity for the fortnight before the filing deadline, without buying more hardware. Which cloud model does it need?
notes.back: C: hybrid cloud.
notes.choices:
A) Multicloud
B) Private cloud only
C) Hybrid cloud
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: staying private means buying hardware for a short peak. C is wrong: multicloud combines public providers and says nothing about the existing private cloud.
notes.explanation: A hybrid cloud lets a private cloud surge into public cloud resources for temporary demand.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Hybrid cloud”

notes.front: A retailer runs its website on one public cloud provider and its analytics on another. Which cloud model is this?

notes.front: A hospital keeps patient records in its own private cloud and runs its public website on a public provider, with the two connected. Which cloud model is this?
notes.back: Hybrid cloud.

notes.front: CapEx or OpEx? A company buys a rack of servers and pays to fit out a new server room.
notes.back: CapEx: up-front spending on physical infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Servers and datacentre space bought in advance are the textbook examples of capital expenditure.

notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: CapEx or OpEx? A company pays a monthly bill for the cloud storage it used that month.
notes.back: OpEx: ongoing spending on a service as it is consumed.
notes.explanation: Paying for cloud services as you consume them is classed as operational expenditure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under pay-as-you-go pricing, a firm uses twice as much compute in March as in February. What happens to its March bill?
notes.back: It rises: you pay more in a billing cycle in which you use more.
notes.explanation: Pay-as-you-go charges for what was used during each billing cycle.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure, “Consumption”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A research lab finishes a month-long simulation run on cloud machines. Under the consumption-based model, what should it do with them, and why?
notes.back: Release them; once released it stops paying, since you pay only for what you use.
notes.explanation: Renting and releasing capacity, instead of owning it, is the core of the consumption-based model.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe the consumption-based model, “Describe the consumption-based model”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A payroll system runs on the same virtual machine size in the same region around the clock, and will for the next three years. Which pricing option gives the deepest discount?
notes.back: A: Azure Reservations.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Reservations
B) Pay-as-you-go
C) Azure Spot Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: it gives no commitment discount. C is wrong: payroll cannot tolerate eviction at 30 seconds’ notice.
notes.explanation: Reservations lock in savings for a specific resource, size and region, deliver deeper discounts, and work best with stable usage.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “How do savings plans compare with reservations?”

notes.evidence: Reservations lock in savings for a specific resource, size, and region, which delivers deeper discounts but works best when usage is stable and predictable.

notes.front: A software firm spends a steady amount on compute each hour, but keeps moving workloads between machine sizes, regions and compute services. Which commitment suits it?
notes.back: A: Azure savings plan for compute.
notes.choices:
A) Azure savings plan for compute
B) Azure Reservations
C) Azure Spot Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a reservation is tied to one resource, size and region. C is wrong: Spot is not a commitment and can be evicted.
notes.explanation: A savings plan is a per-hour spend commitment that applies automatically across eligible services and regions, which suits changing workloads.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are savings plans?, “How do savings plans compare with reservations?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Savings plans are based on a dollar‑per‑hour spend commitment and automatically apply across eligible services and regions, making them ideal for changing or dynamic workloads.

notes.front: An animation studio renders frames overnight; if a machine disappears, the job just picks up the frame again later. It wants the lowest price and makes no long-term commitment. Which option fits?
notes.back: C: Azure Spot Virtual Machines.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Reservations
B) Azure savings plan for compute
C) Azure Spot Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: both need a one- or three-year commitment, which the studio does not want.
notes.explanation: Spot machines are suited to workloads that can handle interruptions, such as batch processing jobs.

notes.front: A charity’s website must resize each uploaded photo, a job that takes about a second and happens a few dozen times a day. Why is serverless computing a good fit?
notes.back: An upload event wakes the code, it runs briefly, and the charity pays only while it runs.
notes.explanation: Short event-driven work suits functions, and billing covers only processor time while the function runs.

notes.front: Public cloud versus private cloud: who can use it, and who controls it?
notes.back: Public: anyone who buys, on a provider’s infrastructure. Private: one organisation only, with much greater control for its own team.
notes.explanation: Openness to the general public is the key difference; the private cloud trades cost for control.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Public cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Hybrid cloud versus multicloud: what does each combine?
notes.back: Hybrid: a public cloud with a private cloud. Multicloud: two or more public cloud providers.
notes.explanation: The two are easily confused, but only hybrid involves a private cloud.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Define cloud models, “Multicloud”

notes.front: CapEx versus OpEx: when is the money spent, and on what?
notes.back: CapEx: up front, on physical infrastructure. OpEx: over time, on services as they are used.
notes.explanation: Cloud spending falls on the OpEx side because it is paid as consumed.

notes.front: Savings plan versus reservation: what is committed, and which suits which workload?
notes.back: Savings plan: an hourly spend, across services and regions, for changing workloads. Reservation: a specific resource, size and region, for stable usage.
notes.explanation: Reservations deliver deeper discounts but work best when usage is stable and predictable.

notes.evidence: Savings plans are based on a dollar‑per‑hour spend commitment and automatically apply across eligible services and regions, making them ideal for changing or dynamic workloads.

notes.front: Virtual machine versus serverless function: when must resources be running?
notes.back: A virtual machine must keep running for the app to work; a serverless function is woken by an event and released afterwards.
notes.explanation: Serverless removes the need to keep resources provisioned when there are no events.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe Azure functions, “Describe Azure functions”

notes.front: Pay-as-you-go versus a reservation: what do you commit to, and what do you get?
notes.back: Pay-as-you-go: no commitment, pay per use. Reservation: a one- or three-year commitment in return for a discount.
notes.explanation: Without a reservation, continuously running services are charged at pay-as-you-go rates.
notes.source: Azure documentation: What are Azure Reservations?, “Why buy a reservation?”
